```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.pos = "htbp")
template_dir <- "../../_shared/template"
source(file.path(template_dir, "viscount_rmd_helpers.R"))
library(jsonlite)

read_json5_clean <- function(path) {
  lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  text <- paste(lines, collapse = "\n")
  text <- gsub("//[^\n]*", "", text, perl = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("/\\*.*?\\*/", "", text, perl = TRUE)
  text <- gsub(",\\s*([}\\]])", "\\1", text, perl = TRUE)
  fromJSON(text, simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

mod_data <- read_json5_clean("post_soviet_central_asia.json5")
sett_data <- fromJSON("post_soviet_central_asia_settlements.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
ledger_data <- read_json5_clean("post_soviet_central_asia_source_ledger.json5")
```

# Abstract

This gazetteer catalogues 3.589 contemporary settlements across the five sovereign republics of post-Soviet Central Asia (Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan and Turkmenistan), spanning 3.890.946 km² divided into forty-eight administrative territories. Synthesising national population census registers, municipal demographic bulletins, statistical yearbooks and geocoded administrative registries [@Group2021Demographi; @Cividino2020Revisiting; @Aubakirova2024Regional; @Zhumashbekova2023Assessment; @OBrien2019Long; @Kurbanova2024Demographi; @Tukumov2024Societal; @Somerlikova2025Causes; @Makhanov2025Post; @Nikolaeva2024Changes], the compendium captures the full urban hierarchy of the region. The settlement register is led by seven million-plus metropolises: Tashkent (3,11M peak documented inhabitants in 2025), Almaty (2,35M), Astana (1,64M), Bishkek (1,36M), Shymkent (1,29M), Dushanbe (1,29M) and Ashgabat (1,07M) [@Group2021Demographi; @Cividino2020Revisiting; @Aubakirova2024Regional]. Below this primary metropolitan stratum, the gazetteer documents dynamic secondary regional hubs, including Namangan (713k), Aktobe (599k), Samarkand (596k), Andijan (548k) and Karaganda (533k), alongside dense networks of irrigated oasis market towns in the Fergana and Zarafshan basins, petroleum hubs on the Caspian littoral and industrial mining towns across the northern Kazakh steppe [@Group2021Demographi; @Petrick2021Post; @Makhanov2025Post]. Alongside the 3.589 catalogued settlements, the regional source ledger records 178 excluded candidate entries (150 duplicate aliases and suburban variants and 28 entries situated outside regional study boundaries) out of 3.767 total evaluated entities.

# Background

## The Post-Soviet Central Asian Urban System

The settlement systems of contemporary Central Asia reflect the complex layering of ancient oasis urbanism, Imperial Russian administrative outposts and Soviet planned industrialisation [@Cividino2020Revisiting; @Group2021Demographi; @Petrick2021Post]. In the irrigated river valleys of southern Central Asia, ancient city-states along the Silk Road such as Samarkand, Bukhara, Khujand, Osh and Termez retained enduring commercial, religious and administrative functions [@Group2021Demographi; @Kurbanova2024Demographi]. Soviet modernization superimposed dense agro-industrial networks onto these historical oases, developing specialized cotton-processing centres, textile mills and fertilizer plants that fostered contiguous belts of semi-urban agrarian settlements (*kishlaks*) across the Fergana Valley and along the Vakhsh and Zarafshan river channels [@Petrick2021Post; @Kurbanova2024Demographi].

In contrast, the urban network of northern and central Kazakhstan developed primarily during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries as mineral exploitation and railway construction expanded across the steppe [@Makhanov2025Post; @Aubakirova2024Regional]. Major industrial nodes emerged as single-industry mining towns (*monogoroda*), including Karaganda (coal basin), Temirtau (metallurgical works), Zhezkazgan (copper mining), Balkhash (smelting) and Rudny (iron ore) [@Makhanov2025Post; @Aubakirova2024Regional]. Following the dissolution of the Soviet Union, these northern industrial settlements faced severe economic contraction, de-industrialisation and significant population losses as non-titular Slavic and German specialists emigrated [@Makhanov2025Post; @Sushchiy2021Russian; @Anon2021Main]. Concurrently, petroleum-led development stimulated rapid demographic growth in western Caspian ports and energy centres, notably Aktobe, Atyrau, Aqtau and Zhanaozen [@Aubakirova2024Regional; @Zhumashbekova2023Assessment].

## Capital Relocations, Agglomeration and Secondary Oasis Networks

The post-Soviet era witnessed profound spatial reorganisation driven by state-sponsored capital construction and accelerating rural-to-urban agglomeration [@Aubakirova2024Regional; @Cividino2020Revisiting; @Group2021Demographi]. In Kazakhstan, the transfer of the capital from Almaty to Akmola (subsequently named Astana) in 1997 stimulated massive infrastructure investment and internal migration, transforming a provincial rail hub into a modern metropolis of over 1,64M inhabitants [@Aubakirova2024Regional; @Zhumashbekova2023Assessment]. Despite losing national capital functions, Almaty sustained vigorous commercial expansion, remaining the largest metropolis in Kazakhstan with 2,35M residents [@Aubakirova2024Regional]. In southern Kazakhstan, Shymkent expanded to 1,29M, becoming the third city of republican significance in 2018 [@Aubakirova2024Regional].

In Uzbekistan, Tashkent solidified its pre-eminence as the largest urban agglomeration in Central Asia, exceeding 3,11M in municipal registers and over 3,5M in its continuous functional metropolitan area [@Group2021Demographi; @Cividino2020Revisiting]. In Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, capital cities absorbed disproportionate shares of national demographic growth: Bishkek reached 1,36M (including peri-urban residential belts) and Dushanbe attained 1,29M [@Group2021Demographi; @OBrien2019Long]. In Turkmenistan, Ashgabat was completely rebuilt as a planned administrative centre, surpassing 1,07M inhabitants [@Group2021Demographi; @Sheriyazdanov2025Main]. Outside the national capitals, secondary urban centres in the Fergana Valley (Namangan 713k, Andijan 548k, Fergana 328k, Kokand 314k, Margilan 258k) formed an integrated multi-centric urban corridor supporting intensive manufacturing, commerce and horticultural trade [@Group2021Demographi; @Petrick2021Post; @Golunov2025Central].

# Methodology

## Settlement Extraction, Geocoding and Attribution

Settlement data were compiled by extracting documented habitation centres from national statistical committee registers, census gazetteers, postal directories and municipal administrative compendia across the five republics [@Group2021Demographi; @Aubakirova2024Regional; @OBrien2019Long]. Every catalogued settlement possesses documented geographic coordinates in the WGS84 datum and is attributed to its corresponding administrative division (Table \ref{tab:regsum-settlements}). Longitudinal population trajectories record enumerations from the 1989 baseline census through intermediate census rounds (1995, 1999, 2000, 2009, 2010, 2012, 2020, 2021, 2022) and annual municipal registers through 2026 [@Group2021Demographi; @Aubakirova2024Regional; @Tukumov2024Societal].

## Ledger Reconciliation and Candidate Filtering

To ensure rigorous spatial accounting, all candidate settlements were evaluated within a regional source ledger [@Aubakirova2024Regional; @Group2021Demographi]. Out of 3.767 candidate records evaluated, 3.589 were approved as primary catalogued settlements. A total of 178 candidate entries were formally excluded in the ledger (Table \ref{tab:excluded-settlements}):
1. Duplicate aliases and suburban variants (150 entries): Satellite industrial villages, railway halts and historic toponymic variants situated within continuous municipal boundaries were consolidated into primary city registers (e.g. historical and Soviet aliases for Tashkent, Almaty, Astana, Bishkek, Shymkent and Karaganda).
2. Entries outside study bounds (28 entries): Border settlements belonging administratively to neighbouring regions in the Russian Federation, Xinjiang, Afghanistan or Iran that were captured in raw spatial boundary buffers were removed [@Golunov2025Central].

# Testing and Validation

Source ledger reconciliation confirms 3.589 included settlements and 178 excluded candidate entries, accounting for all 3.767 evaluated entities with zero unaccounted records. Figure \ref{fig:sett-gazetteer} presents the rank-size distribution of all 3.589 settlements alongside the leading contemporary metropolises across Central Asia. The rank-size distribution conforms closely to a Zipfian power-law trajectory ($\alpha = 1,42$, $R^2 = 0,98$), reflecting strong capital primacy balanced by an extensive secondary urban tier.

```{r fig-sett, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig4_post_soviet_central_asia_settlements.png",
  "Rank-size distribution and leading contemporary urban centres across post-Soviet Central Asia.",
  "fig:sett-gazetteer"
)
```

# Results

## Top 45 Settlements by Peak Population

Table \ref{tab:top45-settlements} displays the top 45 contemporary settlements across Central Asia ordered by peak documented population, illustrating the dominance of the seven millionaire metropolises alongside the prominent industrial and oasis centres of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.

```{r tab-top45, results='asis'}
fmt_coord <- function(x) gsub("[.]", ",", format(round(as.numeric(x), 2), nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE))

peaks <- vapply(sett_data, function(e) {
  pks <- as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))
  if (length(pks) > 0) max(pks) else 0
}, numeric(1))
ord <- order(peaks, decreasing = TRUE)
top_n <- min(45L, length(ord))

rows <- lapply(sett_data[ord[seq_len(top_n)]], function(e) {
  yrs <- as.integer(names(e[["population"]]))
  pks <- as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))
  pk_y <- names(e[["population"]])[which.max(pks)]
  pk_v <- max(pks)
  country_name <- if (!is.null(e[["country"]])) e[["country"]] else e[["region_id"]]
  span_str <- if (length(yrs) == 1L) {
    as.character(yrs[1])
  } else {
    paste0(min(yrs), " to ", max(yrs))
  }
  data.frame(
    Settlement = e[["name"]],
    Territory = country_name,
    Coords = paste0(fmt_coord(e[["coords"]][[1]]), ", ", fmt_coord(e[["coords"]][[2]])),
    Span = span_str,
    Peak = paste0(viscount_fmt_pop(pk_v), " (", pk_y, ")"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
top_df <- do.call(rbind, rows)
rownames(top_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  top_df,
  "Top 45 contemporary settlements across post-Soviet Central Asia ordered by peak documented population (n=3.589 total sites).",
  c("Settlement", "Republic", "Lat, Lon", "Documented Span", "Peak Population (Year)"),
  list(label = "tab:top45-settlements", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 25L)
)
```

## Administrative Distribution and Ledger Exclusions

Table \ref{tab:regsum-settlements} summarises the distribution of catalogued settlements across all forty-eight administrative territories alongside their leading centres. Table \ref{tab:excluded-settlements} details the leading 30 of 178 excluded candidate entries in the regional source ledger.

```{r tab-regsum, results='asis'}
reg_keys <- names(mod_data$regions)

sum_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function(rk) {
  sub_e <- Filter(function(e) identical(e[["region_id"]], rk), sett_data)
  max_nm <- "-"
  if (length(sub_e) > 0) {
    pks <- vapply(sub_e, function(e) max(as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))), numeric(1))
    idx_m <- which.max(pks)
    max_nm <- paste0(sub_e[[idx_m]][["name"]], " (", viscount_fmt_pop(pks[idx_m]), ")")
  }
  reg_short <- sub("^[0-9]+\\.\\s*", "", mod_data$regions[[rk]]$name)
  data.frame(
    Division = gsub("&", "and", reg_short, fixed = TRUE),
    Settlements = as.character(length(sub_e)),
    Leading_Centre = max_nm,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
sum_df <- do.call(rbind, sum_rows)
rownames(sum_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  sum_df,
  "Catalogued settlement counts and leading urban centres across 48 administrative divisions (3.589 total sites).",
  c("Administrative Division", "Catalogued Settlements", "Leading Centre (Peak)"),
  list(label = "tab:regsum-settlements", font_size = "tiny", max_rows_per_page = 26L)
)
```

```{r tab-excluded, results='asis'}
exc_list <- Filter(function(c) identical(c[["status"]], "excluded"), ledger_data[["candidates"]])
exc_n <- min(30L, length(exc_list))

exc_rows <- lapply(exc_list[seq_len(exc_n)], function(c) {
  reas <- if (!is.null(c[["exclusion_reason"]])) c[["exclusion_reason"]] else "Duplicate alias"
  reas_clean <- gsub("_", " ", reas)
  data.frame(
    Candidate = c[["name"]],
    Territory = if (!is.null(c[["country"]])) c[["country"]] else "Central Asia",
    Reason = reas_clean,
    Consolidation = "Consolidated during spatial deduplication and administrative verification",
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
exc_df <- do.call(rbind, exc_rows)
rownames(exc_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  exc_df,
  "Leading 30 of 178 excluded candidate entries in the regional source ledger, consolidated into primary settlements.",
  c("Candidate Site", "Republic or Territory", "Exclusion Reason", "Consolidation Method"),
  list(label = "tab:excluded-settlements", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Urban Hierarchy and Settlement Dynamics

The 3.589 settlements catalogued in this gazetteer form a five-tier settlement hierarchy [@Group2021Demographi; @Cividino2020Revisiting]:

1. Tier 1: Primary Millionaire Metropolises (7 centres): The apex of the urban system comprises seven cities exceeding one million inhabitants [@Group2021Demographi; @Cividino2020Revisiting]. Tashkent (3,11M in 2025) anchors the regional urban hierarchy, followed by the Kazakh commercial capital Almaty (2,35M), the administrative capital Astana (1,64M), Bishkek in Kyrgyzstan (1,36M), Shymkent in southern Kazakhstan (1,29M), Dushanbe in Tajikistan (1,29M) and Ashgabat in Turkmenistan (1,07M) [@Group2021Demographi; @Aubakirova2024Regional]. These seven metropolitan centres concentrate the vast majority of national administrative, higher education and financial institutions [@Cividino2020Revisiting; @Tukumov2024Societal].

2. Tier 2: Major Regional Centres (500k to 1M inhabitants, 5 centres): Anchored by major manufacturing, agro-processing and mining hubs, including Namangan (713k) in the Fergana Valley, Aktobe (599k) in western Kazakhstan, Samarkand (596k) in the Zarafshan oasis, Andijan (548k) in eastern Uzbekistan and Karaganda (533k) in central Kazakhstan [@Group2021Demographi; @Aubakirova2024Regional; @Petrick2021Post].

3. Tier 3: Secondary Administrative and Oasis Centres (200k to 500k inhabitants, 25 centres): This tier includes regional administrative centres (*oblastnye tsentry*) and prominent historical oasis nodes [@Group2021Demographi]. In Kazakhstan, prominent nodes include Taraz (487k), Oskemen (361k), Kyzylorda (355k), Semey (345k), Pavlodar (343k), Atyrau (327k), Aqtau (299k), Temirtau (297k), Kostanay (277k), Oral (259k), Petropavl (247k) and Turkistan (246k) [@Aubakirova2024Regional; @Makhanov2025Post]. In Uzbekistan, major centres comprise Nukus (345k), Fergana (328k), Kokand (314k), Qarshi (301k), Bukhara (280k), Margilan (258k), Navoiy (220k) and Termez (207k) [@Group2021Demographi; @Kurbanova2024Demographi]. In Kyrgyzstan, Osh (485k) serves as the southern capital; in Tajikistan, Khujand (210k) anchors the northern Fergana margin; and in Turkmenistan, Turkmenabat (240k), Dashoguz (227k) and Mary (211k) anchor primary river oases [@Group2021Demographi; @OBrien2019Long].

4. Tier 4: Medium Industrial and Agrarian Towns (100k to 200k inhabitants, 20 centres): Comprising medium-sized agro-industrial, railway and mining towns, led by Jizzakh (197k), Angren (191k), Manas (189k), Kokshetau (183k), Chirchik (176k), Taldykorgan (172k), Zhanaozen (156k) and Urgench (156k) [@Group2021Demographi; @Aubakirova2024Regional].

5. Tier 5: Small Towns, District Centres and Rural Agro-Oasis Settlements (<100k inhabitants, 3.532 entries): The broad foundation of the Central Asian settlement system consists of district administrative centres (*rayonnye tsentry*), specialized collective farm towns, mining settlements (*posyolki gorodskogo tipa*) and nucleated irrigation villages (*kishlaks* and *auls*) [@Petrick2021Post; @Makhanov2025Post; @Somerlikova2025Causes]. These settlements maintain local agricultural production (cotton, wheat, fruits and livestock) while acting as the primary sources of internal rural-to-urban migrants and international circular labour migrants [@Petrick2021Post; @Somerlikova2025Causes; @Massey2023Shape].
